characters.description: A musician who recognizes the exceptional quality of Veda's singing voice and helps redirect her ambitions toward classical performance. His professional interest gives Veda a path to status independent of Mildred's restaurants.
characters.name: Carlo Treviso

characters.description: A concert and radio impresario involved in Veda's rise as a singer. He treats her voice as a valuable professional asset and helps move her career beyond her mother's control.
characters.name: Mr Levin

recaps.ending: Mildred discovers that Veda and Monte have become lovers despite Monte's marriage to her. In rage she attacks Veda and injures her throat, apparently threatening the singing career around which the household has been reorganized. The damage proves temporary. Veda recovers and uses the publicity surrounding the incident to strengthen her professional position, then leaves for New York under her management's protection. Mildred can no longer keep the restaurant business functioning after diverting money to the Beragon household and allowing debts and control to slip away; the enterprise passes out of her hands. Her marriage to Monte ends. She returns to Bert, and the two remarry, restoring a partnership stripped of their earlier hopes of prosperity and social ascent. When they learn that Veda has gone without a real reconciliation, Mildred and Bert finally acknowledge the futility of organizing their lives around her approval. They drink together and dismiss her hold over them. The conclusion gives Mildred survival and companionship rather than triumph: she has lost the business she built and the daughter she tried to possess through sacrifice, but she is no longer maintaining the social fantasy that ruined both her work and her judgment.
recaps.in_short: After separating from Bert during the Depression, Mildred Pierce secretly becomes a waitress and builds her talent for pies and chicken dinners into a successful Southern California restaurant business. Her practical ability supports daughters Ray and Veda, but she remains ashamed of service work because haughty, musically gifted Veda despises anything she considers common. Ray's death deepens Mildred's fixation on her surviving child. Mildred becomes involved with impoverished aristocrat Monte Beragon, while Veda fakes a pregnancy to extort money from a wealthy family and is expelled from home. Veda then discovers an exceptional singing voice and returns as a rising performer. To regain her, Mildred marries Monte and spends beyond the restaurants' means to sustain his estate and Veda's ambitions. She eventually discovers Veda and Monte together and injures Veda's throat in an attack, but Veda recovers and leaves for New York. Mildred loses her business, divorces Monte, and remarries Bert. Together they finally reject Veda's power over them.

recaps.text: During the Depression, Mildred Pierce's marriage breaks down after Bert's real-estate business fails and he becomes involved with Maggie Biederhof. Mildred orders him out of their Glendale house and must find a way to support their daughters, the affectionate Ray and the older, socially ambitious Veda. She first tries selling homemade pies but needs steady wages. After discouraging attempts to find respectable office or sales work, she accepts a waitressing job and hides it from Veda, knowing her daughter regards service work as degrading. Mildred learns quickly, aided by Ida Corwin, and discovers that tips plus sales of her pies can provide a reliable income. Wally Burgan, Bert's former partner, remains in her orbit as both an adviser and a lover, while neighbor Lucy Gessler supplies blunt practical counsel. Mildred's competence begins creating a new life, but her secrecy reveals the central weakness in her independence: she measures success through Veda's class prejudices rather than through the security her work actually provides.

Veda discovers Mildred's waitress uniform and treats her mother's work with contempt. Mildred responds not by rejecting Veda's values but by trying to create a business impressive enough to win her respect. Building on the popularity of her pies and her knowledge of restaurant service, she opens a Glendale restaurant centered on chicken dinners and waffles. The venture succeeds, and Mildred begins expanding, proving herself a skilled operator in purchasing, staffing, cooking, and promotion. Her household, however, suffers a devastating loss when Ray becomes ill and dies. Grief leaves Mildred even more emotionally dependent on Veda, the surviving child. Through Wally's social connections she meets Monte Beragon, whose inherited Pasadena name and estate conceal a shortage of money. Mildred is attracted to his polish and to the world he represents. Their affair gives her access to the social standing Veda admires, but it also links her hard-earned income to a man whose way of life depends on wealth he no longer possesses.

Mildred's restaurants continue to prosper, but her relationships with Monte and Veda become increasingly costly. Monte's indolence and his willingness to accept Mildred's support eventually sour the romance, and she draws away from him. Veda, meanwhile, claims that she is pregnant by Sammy Forrester and uses the threat of scandal to obtain money from his wealthy family. When Mrs Forrester investigates, the pregnancy is exposed as a calculated fiction. Mildred is appalled not only by the fraud but by Veda's cold pride in having made money through it. She drives Veda from the house. The separation that Mildred means as punishment instead frees Veda from dependence on her. Veda begins performing popular music and then attracts attention for an exceptional classical singing voice. With professional instruction and management, she gains the prospect of a lucrative public career. Mildred has built a growing business through labor, but Veda now has a route to money and prestige that more closely matches her own ambitions.

Veda's voice brings rapid professional advancement in concerts and radio. Mildred longs to restore their relationship and is willing to reorganize her life around that goal. Because Veda values the Beragon name and estate, Mildred renews her connection with Monte and marries him, effectively purchasing entry into his social world with income from her restaurants. Veda returns to the household, but the reconciliation leaves the old balance of power intact: Mildred supplies money while seeking affection, and Veda accepts comfort without surrendering control. Maintaining the Pasadena estate, Monte's habits, and Veda's career places increasing strain on the restaurant company. Mildred conceals transfers and financial trouble rather than reduce the display that has brought her daughter home. The practical discipline that created her success gives way to desperate spending. Friends and business associates see the danger more clearly than she does, while Mildred continues to treat the preservation of the household as proof that her years of work and sacrifice have achieved their purpose.

Mildred's attempt to sustain the Beragon household brings her restaurant business to crisis. She then discovers that Veda and Monte are lovers. The betrayal collapses both the marriage and Mildred's belief that sacrifice can secure Veda's loyalty. She attacks her daughter and injures Veda's throat, seemingly endangering the voice on which Veda's new independence depends. The injury is temporary, and Veda's managers turn the surrounding attention to her advantage. She recovers and leaves for New York to continue her career, without giving Mildred the reconciliation she wants. The restaurants pass beyond Mildred's control after the financial damage caused by her diversions and neglect. Her marriage to Monte ends, and the social position she bought through him disappears. Mildred returns to Bert, and they remarry. When they receive confirmation that Veda has gone, the reunited couple finally voice their rejection of the daughter whose standards and approval have governed them. Mildred ends without her business or her imagined place in high society, but with Bert and with a clearer recognition of the obsession that undid her achievements.

characters.description: A small, nameless boy surviving on the streets of Warsaw by taking food and running. He knows almost nothing about his past or the world beyond immediate sights and needs, and he initially understands himself through the names other people shout at him.
characters.name: Misha

characters.description: An older red-haired street boy who catches the nameless child after a theft. Quick, commanding, and far more aware of the danger around them, he takes charge of the younger boy and brings him among other homeless children.
characters.name: Uri

characters.description: One of the orphan boys in Uri's group, which shelters together and survives by stealing. He is wary of the strange newcomer and participates in the group's rough efforts to test and teach him.
characters.name: Kuba

characters.description: A member of Uri's band of homeless boys. Like the others, he relies on the group for protection and food amid the invasion and treats survival knowledge as more useful than the newcomer's questions.
characters.name: Enos

characters.description: One of the street children living under Uri's informal leadership in wartime Warsaw. He shares the boys' hiding place and their dangerous routine of finding food.
characters.name: Ferdi

characters.description: A boy in Uri's group of young thieves and refugees. His place among them makes him part of the nameless child's first remembered community.
characters.name: Olek

characters.description: A large boy in the band of homeless children who shelter together. His simple descriptive nickname is typical of the identities the boys use among themselves.
characters.name: Big Henry

characters.description: A small, determined Jewish girl from a Warsaw family. Curious about the street boy who appears near her home, she can be imperious and bold, and she refuses to remain merely an observer of his freedom.
characters.name: Janina Milgrom

characters.description: Janina's father, a Jewish man trying to keep his family together as German restrictions tighten. He responds to the street boy with patience and gives him a place within the family's increasingly precarious life.
characters.name: Mr. Milgrom

characters.description: Janina's mother, whose declining health adds to the Milgrom family's vulnerability. She lives with her family under the restrictions imposed on Warsaw's Jews.
characters.name: Mrs. Milgrom

characters.description: A relative living with the Milgrom family. Anxious to find a rule or identity that will protect him, he follows rumors about how one might escape the persecution aimed at Jews.
characters.name: Uncle Shepsel

characters.description: A large German guard feared by children in the ghetto for his violence. His presence near the wall makes even the routines of smuggling food more dangerous.
characters.name: Buffo

characters.description: The adult who cares for a group of Jewish orphans in the ghetto. He remains responsible for the children as conditions worsen and the occupation closes around them.
characters.name: Janusz Korczak

characters.description: A woman Misha meets years after the war in America. She is drawn to the ceaseless stories of the street seller who calls himself Jack and briefly offers him an ordinary adult life.
characters.name: Vivian

characters.description: The grown daughter who comes into Misha's life after many years of separation. Her arrival gives him a living connection to a family he did not know and a chance to be known outside his wartime memories.
characters.name: Katherine

characters.description: Katherine's young daughter and Misha's granddaughter. She gives the aging survivor an affectionate family name and listens without demanding that his memories follow an orderly form.
characters.name: Wendy

recaps.ending: During the destruction of the Warsaw ghetto, Misha sees Janina forced toward a deportation train and tries to reach her. Uri, now wearing a German uniform, shoots Misha through the ear. The wound keeps him from boarding the train and is Uri's harsh means of saving him. Misha survives outside Warsaw, but he never finds Janina or the rest of the Milgrom family. After the war he wanders and eventually emigrates to the United States, where he sells goods and compulsively tells fragments of his past under the name Jack. He marries Vivian, but trauma makes a stable marriage impossible, and she leaves while pregnant. Decades later their adult daughter Katherine finds him. She brings her own daughter, Wendy, into his life. Wendy calls him Poppynoodle, an affectionate identity neither imposed by enemies nor invented for survival. Katherine gives Wendy the middle name Janina, preserving the child Misha lost. In the granddaughter's acceptance and the new family name, he finally gains a home for his memories and a belonging that survives them.
recaps.in_short: A nameless child thief survives the German invasion of Warsaw with Uri and a band of street boys. Uri gives him the invented identity Misha Pilsudski and says he is a Gypsy. Misha befriends Jewish girl Janina Milgrom and joins her family when they are imprisoned in the Warsaw ghetto. Small enough to slip through gaps in the wall, he smuggles food and Janina begins following him, while hunger, disease, killings, and deportations destroy their world. When Janina is driven toward a transport train, Misha tries to follow. Uri, disguised as a German soldier, shoots him to keep him off the train, saving his life. Misha never recovers the Milgroms. He eventually moves to America, takes the name Jack, marries briefly, and remains haunted by the past. Much later his daughter Katherine finds him and introduces his granddaughter Wendy, who calls him Poppynoodle and receives Janina as a middle name. Their love gives the aging survivor a final name connected to family rather than persecution.

recaps.text: A very small boy steals bread in Warsaw and runs whenever people shout after him. He has no known name, family, or history. Uri, an older red-haired street child, catches him, feeds him, and brings him to a hidden group of orphan boys who survive by theft. German forces invade the city, but the younger child lacks the knowledge to understand bombs, soldiers, Jews, or the danger represented by the marching men he admires. Uri tries to teach him caution and constructs a past for him: he calls the boy Misha Pilsudski and says he belongs to a wandering Gypsy family. The story gives Misha an identity to repeat even though he cannot distinguish memory from Uri's invention. As occupation transforms Warsaw, Misha continues to experience events through hunger, speed, bright objects, and the names other people provide.

Misha meets Janina Milgrom, a small Jewish girl whose family still has a home and possessions. He visits the family and becomes attached to Janina despite their quarrels. German rules increasingly isolate and humiliate Jewish residents, requiring identifying armbands and taking away ordinary freedoms. Misha is told that his invented Gypsy identity places him in danger too, but he still fails to grasp the system behind the violence. The Milgroms and other Jewish families are forced into the crowded Warsaw ghetto. Misha goes with them and is accepted into their household, gaining the nearest thing to a family he has known. Behind the walls, hunger and fear replace his earlier freedom to range through the city, though his size and street skills remain possible means of survival.

Life in the ghetto contracts around hunger, sickness, cold, and arbitrary German violence. Misha discovers openings through which his small body can pass under or through the wall. He resumes stealing on the other side and carries food back to the Milgrom household. Janina insists on following him. What begins for her as a thrilling imitation of Misha becomes a dangerous routine essential to the family. Misha moves between the imprisoned community and the larger city, but this mobility cannot make him understand or stop what is happening. The orphan boys are scattered by the worsening conditions, and every trip risks guards, patrols, and the closing of escape routes. The adults' efforts to follow rules or find exemptions offer no reliable protection.

The ghetto's inhabitants continue to die from starvation, disease, exposure, and shootings. Misha and Janina keep smuggling as long as they can, becoming bolder even as the walls are more closely watched. The death of Olek, displayed as a warning after he is caught, shows the children what capture means. Buffo and other German guards make the wall a place of terror. Janina's behavior becomes increasingly desperate and defiant, while the Milgrom family loses health and hope. Uncle Shepsel's attempts to adopt a protected identity cannot halt the persecution. Misha remains devoted to Janina and her father, but his ability to bring scraps of food into the ghetto is no answer to the organized destruction closing in on them.

German forces empty the ghetto, driving Jewish residents into the streets and toward deportation trains. Families and orphaned children are marched away under guard. Misha tries to stay with the Milgroms and searches amid the violence for Janina. He sees her being forced toward a boxcar and runs after her, intending to follow wherever she is taken. Uri appears in a German uniform and shoots Misha through the ear. The attack knocks him down and prevents him from boarding the train; beneath the disguise, Uri has used the only method available to save him. Misha survives the wound, but Janina, her father, and the others are carried away. He is left outside the transport system that has swallowed the family he chose, with no way to learn their fate or restore the ghetto community.

Misha survives the remainder of the war but never recovers Janina or the Milgrom family. He wanders after the occupation ends and eventually emigrates to the United States. An official gives him the name Jack, and he makes a living selling goods while pouring out disordered memories to strangers. Vivian listens, marries him, and becomes pregnant, but Misha's trauma and inability to settle into ordinary life contribute to her departure. Many years later, his adult daughter Katherine finds him and introduces her daughter Wendy. Wendy accepts his stories and calls him Poppynoodle, giving him a name rooted in affection. Katherine gives the child Janina as a middle name. The new family cannot undo Misha's losses, but it preserves Janina's name and lets him end his life as a father and grandfather rather than only as the nameless boy, Misha, or Jack.

characters.description: A surgically altered duplicate of Admiral Naismith who takes command of the Ariel by deception. He orders an unauthorized expedition to Jackson's Hole to remove clone children from a lethal transplant program.
characters.name: Naismith impersonator

characters.description: Captain of the Dendarii cruiser Ariel. Bel accepts the apparent Admiral Naismith's urgent plan to raid a Jackson's Hole clone facility and rescue children destined for brain-transplant procedures, despite knowing that Naismith has a clone.
characters.name: Bel Thorne

characters.description: A towering, genetically engineered Dendarii commando assigned to Green Squad. She is personally close to the officer she believes is Naismith and joins his armed descent on the clone facility, unaware that the mission rests on an impersonation.
characters.name: Genetically altered sergeant

characters.description: The Barrayaran Imperial Security operative behind the Admiral Naismith identity and commander of the Dendarii. Back on Escobar, he discovers that his clone brother stole the Ariel and departed for Jackson's Hole.
characters.name: Miles Naismith Vorkosigan

characters.description: A Dendarii captain and Miles's lover. She intends to remain a spacefaring commander rather than enter Barrayaran aristocratic life, and she joins Miles when the stolen Ariel forces an immediate pursuit.
characters.name: Elli Quinn

characters.description: Captain of the Peregrine and one of the Dendarii officers trusted with Miles's dual identity. She helps assess the theft of the Ariel and the danger posed by Miles's impersonator, then remains with the fleet as Miles prepares his response.
characters.name: Elena Bothari-Jesek

characters.description: The officer responsible for Dendarii fleet engineering, as well as Elena Bothari-Jesek's husband and an insider to Miles's identities. He helps plan the response to the Ariel crisis while other obligations continue.
characters.name: Baz Jesek

characters.description: The Komarran conspirator who directed the project that created Miles's clone brother. His group altered the clone's body and used coercion and abuse while training him to replace and assassinate Miles for an old political revenge plot.
characters.name: Ser Galen

characters.description: Miles's engineered clone brother and the man who impersonated Naismith to launch the clone rescue. Trapped with the raiders and children, Mark becomes the person Miles refuses to surrender to Vasa Luigi.
characters.name: Mark

characters.description: The Jacksonian house leader whose forces have surrounded the stranded Dendarii raiders. A long-term user of clone bodies, he is willing to ransom the soldiers while keeping Mark, whose unusual origin makes him especially valuable.
characters.name: Vasa Luigi

characters.description: A Dendarii medic who becomes separated from the retreat with Miles's cryo-chamber. Norwood is found dead after the withdrawal, while both Miles and the chamber remain missing.
characters.name: Medic Norwood

characters.description: One of the rescued clone women aboard the Dendarii ships. She has been taught to expect reunion with a maternal figure and does not yet understand that her creators intended to use her body in a fatal transplant.
characters.name: Marie

characters.description: Chief of Barrayaran Imperial Security. He receives the report that Miles was frozen after a chest wound but lost with his cryo-chamber, then assumes responsibility for both the search and the rescued clones.
characters.name: Simon Illyan

characters.description: The genetic mother of Miles and Mark. She welcomes Mark as a separate and equally valid son, insists that his choices need not be limited to replacing his missing brother, and offers him family recognition under the clone law of Beta Colony.
characters.name: Cordelia Vorkosigan

characters.description: The genetic father of Miles and Mark. He holds both the Vorkosigan countship and Barrayar's premiership. He accepts Mark's independent responsibility for the clone rescue and explains the succession burden that may follow if Miles cannot return.
characters.name: Aral Vorkosigan

characters.description: The Barrayaran Emperor. In a private audience, he encourages Mark to seek a purpose separate from being Miles's substitute and treats political rank as a responsibility a person can learn to carry. He also gives Mark a direct means of contacting him.
characters.name: Emperor Gregor

characters.description: Miles and Mark's cousin and the fallback family heir. Although still resentful over an earlier conflict with Mark, Ivan escorts him through the capital and protects him during his introduction to Barrayaran public life.
characters.name: Ivan Vorpatril

characters.description: A student with strong academic ambitions whom Mark meets at an Imperial celebration. She plans further study on Beta Colony and responds to Mark as an individual rather than treating him as a copy of Miles.
characters.name: Young woman at Imperial celebration

characters.description: A physician in a hidden collective of cloned medical siblings. She oversees the difficult revival of an unidentified cryo-patient whose replacement organs are still developing and whose autobiographical memory is absent.
characters.name: Rowan

characters.description: The senior figure in a concealed clinic staffed by cloned medical siblings. Her collective has revived a badly wounded amnesiac and is waiting to learn whether his identity and recovered memories can protect their interests.
characters.name: Clone medical collective leader

characters.description: A Jacksonian clone-house baron, long-term user of replacement bodies, and past enemy of Admiral Naismith. Naismith's earlier destruction of his genetic holdings and rescue of a captive give Ryoval a strong motive for revenge.
characters.name: Baron Ryoval

characters.description: A Jacksonian baron associated with the hidden clone medical collective. The group's old ties to him make its clinic Mark's strongest lead to the missing cryo-patient, though its present loyalty is uncertain.
characters.name: Baron Fell

characters.description: A physician from the clone medical collective held under guarded hospitality by Vasa Luigi. She recognizes a conditioned servant in the house as her own younger duplicate and rejects an offer to remain there in a privileged medical post.
characters.name: Collective leader's surgeon sister

characters.description: A young captive clone conditioned to regard the destruction of her own mind as service to her creator. Her resemblance to the collective leader's surgeon sister exposes the transplant plan intended for her body.
characters.name: Clone servant

characters.description: Separate protective responses that emerge within Mark under sustained torture. Three call themselves Gorge, Grunt, and Howl, while a fourth remains unnamed. They divide different forms of harm and shield his core identity from direct awareness.
characters.name: Protective personae

characters.description: Mark's collective name for the four survival personae that protected him during Ryoval's torture. He understands Gorge, Grunt, Howl, and Killer as parts of a single adaptive system rather than identities he intends to erase.
characters.name: Black Gang

characters.description: The aspiring scholar Mark first met at an Imperial celebration. She finds Mark interesting as an individual, and their developing relationship rests on patient trust while she prepares for offworld study.
characters.name: Kareen

recaps.ending: Ryoval is dead, killed by Mark's Killer persona, and Baron Fell gains access to his half-brother's holdings after accepting Mark's exchange. In return, the clone medical collective leaves Jackson's Hole for Escobar with funding and Dendarii protection. The earlier rescued clones receive long-term support from money Mark places in escrow, and he invests in medical work intended to replace lethal brain transplantation. Bel Thorne leaves Dendarii command and may pursue Imperial Security work. Elli Quinn and Elena Bothari-Jesek remain trusted allies, while Miles and Quinn's conflicting hopes for their future remain unresolved. Aral Vorkosigan is recovering from a heart transplant. Miles survives cryo-amnesia and captivity but conceals convulsions and worries about lasting memory damage while awaiting medical clearance. Mark accepts the Black Gang as part of himself and plans confidential therapy, college, and eventual work as an intelligence analyst. He and Miles settle into a more equal brotherhood, and Mark begins a cautious, family-supported relationship with Kareen.
recaps.in_short: Mark, Miles Vorkosigan's engineered clone brother, steals a Dendarii cruiser to save children raised as replacement bodies. Miles pursues him, is gravely wounded during the extraction, and disappears in a cryo-chamber secretly routed to a Jackson's Hole medical collective. While Imperial Security's search falters, Mark gains recognition from the Vorkosigan family and leads a private recovery mission. Revived with amnesia, Miles eventually recovers his identity, while Baron Ryoval captures and tortures Mark. Protective personae called the Black Gang preserve Mark until Killer murders Ryoval. Mark exchanges Ryoval's code keys for the collective's evacuation and financial support. Both brothers return to Barrayar. Miles remains on medical leave with convulsions and memory fears, while Mark funds the rescued clones and a safer medical venture, plans therapy and study, and begins building a relationship with Kareen.

recaps.text: Previously: Miles Vorkosigan, a Barrayaran lord and Imperial Security operative, also commands the Dendarii mercenaries as Admiral Naismith. A Komarran conspiracy led by Ser Galen created a clone from Miles's genetic material, altered him to resemble Miles, and trained him through coercion to serve as an assassin and replacement. Miles regards this young man as his brother despite the hostility created by that abuse. Miles's closest Dendarii associates include his lover and fellow commander Elli Quinn, Captain Elena Bothari-Jesek, and Ariel captain Bel Thorne. His military identity and his place in the Vorkosigan family remain intertwined with Barrayaran security and succession.

An unnamed duplicate of Admiral Naismith takes the Dendarii cruiser Ariel and orders Bel Thorne and Green Squad toward Jackson's Hole. His purpose is to remove dozens of clone children before their bodies are used in brain-transplant operations. The real Admiral Naismith is Miles Vorkosigan, and the impostor is his surgically altered clone brother, once conditioned by Ser Galen to replace him. Miles and Elli Quinn pursue in the Peregrine while other Dendarii obligations continue. At the clone facility, the raiders tell the children what awaits them, but many have been trained to expect loving reunions with their creators and resist evacuation. Security sabotages the Dendarii shuttle and kills its pilot, trapping the assault team with the frightened children. Bel admits that he recognized the impostor before the raid but allowed the rescue effort to proceed. With no transport and hostile forces closing in, he prepares to use surrender negotiations to keep the group alive.

Miles refuses Vasa Luigi's demand that the Dendarii abandon Mark, his clone brother, and mounts an extraction for both the soldiers and the children. During the retreat, Miles suffers a catastrophic chest wound. Elli Quinn places him in the only available cryo-chamber and assumes command, but Medic Norwood becomes separated with the chamber and dies after reporting that the Admiral was sent to safety. Miles and the chamber vanish. The surviving Dendarii reach Fell Station with the rescued children and Vasa Luigi as a hostage. To conceal their weakened position, Quinn, Elena Bothari-Jesek, and Bel Thorne have Mark impersonate Miles during negotiations. Mark cooperates after Elena promises that the children will be protected. Evidence suggests Norwood secretly sent the cryo-chamber through the facility's automated shipping system. With no destination known and local tolerance expiring, the Dendarii exchange their hostage and leave. Forty-nine clones remain with them after one woman returns voluntarily to the house. Mark's attempt to explain the danger to Marie ends in a trauma reaction and a serious violation of her boundaries, and Elena confines him.

At Komarr, Simon Illyan assumes responsibility for locating Miles and finding safe placements for the rescued clones. Mark, ashamed of the failed raid and desperate not to be used as Miles again, deliberately gains weight before Elena escorts him to Barrayar. Cordelia and Aral Vorkosigan receive him as their own son rather than as a substitute. They explain that Miles's permanent loss could leave Mark heir to the countship and exposed to wider succession dangers. Emperor Gregor also meets Mark privately and urges him to develop a purpose of his own, possibly connected to his opposition to the clone trade. Ivan Vorpatril escorts Mark through the capital despite resentment left by an earlier encounter. When residents in a poor district attack Mark as a mutant, his conditioning turns an ordinary fight into nearly lethal violence. Ivan protects his identity and resolves the aftermath. The experience forces Mark to recognize both Barrayar's prejudice and the danger built into his trained responses. Hearing his parents debate his future, he nevertheless begins to believe their acceptance is genuine.

Imperial Security finds Miles's cryo-chamber cleaned and empty in a distant medical inventory, proving it was deliberately moved but not revealing what happened to him. During a family visit, Aral Vorkosigan suffers a cardiac rupture and requires a replacement heart. The political emergency lowers the priority of the already uncertain search. Mark publicly represents his father at the Imperial tax ceremony and increasingly claims the identity of Lord Mark Vorkosigan without asserting Miles's place. At an Imperial celebration he meets a serious prospective student who responds to his distinct identity, but a security leak spreads the belief that Miles is dead and suspicion that Mark harmed the Count. Gregor overrules Illyan and grants Mark access to the raw search files. Mark's analysis leads him to conclude that Norwood kept Miles on Jackson's Hole by sending the chamber to someone with a reason to hide it. Illyan rejects a field mission and also confirms Mark's severe fast-penta allergy. Cordelia instead arranges private transport and permits Mark to recruit volunteers. Elena swears direct service as Mark's armswoman, and the independent search begins to take shape.

A badly wounded man awakens in a secret clinic with replacement organs, no personal memory, and Rowan as his physician. The staff are cloned medical siblings serving a concealed collective associated with Baron Fell. The patient recovers movement, speech, and automatic weapons skills, but fast-penta causes a dangerous reaction and only fragmented memories of Ser Galen and Jackson's Hole. Meanwhile Mark leaves with Elena, Elli Quinn, Bel Thorne, and the genetically altered sergeant. A clue in Norwood's effects connects the missing chamber to the Fell-affiliated clinic, while Baron Ryoval's old grievance against Naismith establishes another danger. The collective leader tells the patient that he must be either Admiral Naismith or Mark Pierre Vorkosigan, but warns that premature clues could create a false identity. Rowan admits that her intimacy with him was partly intended to bind him to the collective, although she also declares genuine feeling. Mark arrives presenting himself as Naismith, and the collective proposes exchanging the missing twin for evacuation. Before an agreement can be reached, armed intruders seize Mark. Rowan flees with the amnesiac patient, but Vasa Luigi's forces capture them both.

House Ryoval captures Mark while mistaking him for Admiral Naismith. Ryoval begins sustained torture meant to destroy his resistance and remake him as a controlled victim. Vasa Luigi separately confines Rowan and the amnesiac, planning to profit from the man's identity. At dinner with the medical collective leader's surgeon sister, a conditioned clone servant is revealed as the sister's younger duplicate and intended replacement body. The patient's memory then returns: he is Miles Naismith Vorkosigan, and Mark took his place after the shooting. Miles conceals this recovery. Under torture, Mark's mind divides the suffering among protective personae - Gorge, Grunt, Howl, and an unnamed fourth presence - while Lord Mark remains sheltered. The surgeon sister and her younger duplicate exploit their resemblance to exchange places, allowing the sister to escape. Miles persuades the servant that she is entitled to her own life, but he is transferred to Ryoval. Before Miles arrives, Ryoval threatens Mark with his brother's capture. The fourth persona, Killer, takes control and kills Ryoval. Mark escapes in the baron's flyer with the code-key ring governing his scattered assets.

Miles reaches Ryoval's abandoned facility, overpowers his guards, and summons help. Elli Quinn, Elena Bothari-Jesek, Bel Thorne, and the altered sergeant arrive, while Mark reports from the medical collective's clinic that he is alive. Mark uses Ryoval's code-key ring as leverage in a negotiation with Baron Fell, Ryoval's half-brother. He gives Fell access to the dead baron's holdings in exchange for the collective's freedom, immediate evacuation to Escobar, and a share of the estate. Both the surgeon sister and the clone servant reach safety. Bel resigns from Dendarii command, and Miles suggests Imperial Security work as another path. Elena destroys Ryoval's recordings of Mark's torture at Mark's request so they cannot become another means of control. Mark calls his four protective personae the Black Gang and regards them as a survival system rather than something to conceal or remove. He commits half of his payment to the rescued clones and plans to invest the rest. Miles and Mark agree that isolated rescues cannot end the transplant trade and that a medical alternative is needed. They leave Jackson's Hole alive and begin relating as adult brothers.

At Winterfair, Miles and Mark appear publicly with Cordelia and the recovering Aral Vorkosigan. Aral has survived his heart transplant, while Cordelia plans a quieter period in the family district and Gregor considers a possible colonial post for him after recovery. Miles expects conditional clearance for duty in two months, but he has concealed convulsions and privately tests his memory because he fears lasting neurological damage. Mark keeps a deliberately distinctive appearance and directs his new wealth toward several purposes. One million Betan dollars remains in escrow for the rescued clones' schooling and welfare, and he invests in the medical collective's offworld venture to develop an alternative to lethal transplant practices. Mark also chooses confidential therapy, accepts the Black Gang as an integral part of himself, and plans college as preparation for navigating Barrayaran society and eventually becoming an Imperial Security analyst. Cordelia conditionally supports his interest in Kareen, provided Mark addresses his trauma and Kareen completes her education. Mark and Kareen begin building trust. Miles and Mark reconcile the consequences of the failed first rescue and return to the district with a more equal relationship.

characters.description: An unnamed New York newspaper employee who writes the paper's advice column under the female pen name Miss Lonelyhearts. The desperate letters sent to the column have stopped feeling like material for a joke, but he has no answer equal to their suffering. He moves between numbness, disgust, drink, and a troubled longing for religious certainty.
characters.name: Miss Lonelyhearts

characters.description: Miss Lonelyhearts's editor, an articulate cynic who treats the advice column and its readers as occasions for cruel comedy. He repeatedly attacks Miss Lonelyhearts's religious impulses and turns earnest feeling into performance.
characters.name: Shrike

characters.description: Miss Lonelyhearts's steady former fiancée. She values ordinary affection, work, and a life away from the newspaper's corrosive atmosphere, and she remains concerned for him despite his volatility.
characters.name: Betty

characters.description: Shrike's wife, whose unhappy marriage places her within the same circle of frustrated desire and emotional cruelty that surrounds Miss Lonelyhearts.
characters.name: Mary Shrike

characters.description: A physically disabled reader who contacts Miss Lonelyhearts after recognizing something of his own pain in the advice column. Awkward and intensely earnest, he wants his suffering to be acknowledged as more than an abstract problem.
characters.name: Peter Doyle

characters.description: Peter Doyle's wife, whom Miss Lonelyhearts meets when he visits the couple. Restless and sexually aggressive, she draws him into another encounter in which his wish to help becomes entangled with appetite, contempt, and shame.
characters.name: Fay Doyle

recaps.ending: After withdrawing from work and passing through a fever, Miss Lonelyhearts believes he has attained the religious certainty he has been seeking. Peter Doyle comes to confront him with a gun after Fay has represented their encounter as an assault. Seeing Doyle approach, Miss Lonelyhearts interprets him not as a threat but as someone he can finally embrace and heal. He rushes toward Doyle; in the struggle, the gun fires. The two men fall together down the stairs. The attempted act of universal love therefore ends in violence, leaving Miss Lonelyhearts's hoped-for redemption inseparable from the delusion and suffering that have pursued him throughout the novella.
recaps.in_short: A young male newspaper writer works under the name Miss Lonelyhearts, answering letters from readers whose poverty, illness, abuse, and loneliness overwhelm the column's conventional advice. His editor, Shrike, mocks both the correspondents and the writer's increasingly desperate religious search. Miss Lonelyhearts alternates between drinking, cruelty, retreat with his former fiancée Betty, and failed attempts to make contact with other sufferers. He befriends Peter Doyle, a disabled reader, and visits Doyle's wife Fay, but the encounter turns sexual and violent. After illness and isolation, Miss Lonelyhearts becomes convinced that he has found a redeeming love. Doyle then arrives with a gun, believing his wife has been attacked. Miss Lonelyhearts rushes to embrace him as a person he can save; the gun discharges and the men tumble down the stairs, turning his vision of salvation into the final catastrophe.

recaps.text: A young man writes a newspaper advice column under the name Miss Lonelyhearts. The letters describe damaged bodies, broken families, poverty, and isolation with a seriousness that defeats the stock consolations he is expected to provide. His editor, Shrike, makes a spectacle of this misery and mocks the writer's impulse to seek a Christian answer. Miss Lonelyhearts feels trapped between the newspaper's cynical pose and a faith he cannot securely inhabit. His distress begins to affect his body, his drinking, and his relations with other people, including Betty, the woman from whom he has separated.

The suffering in the letters continues to invade Miss Lonelyhearts's life, but his efforts to escape it reproduce the cruelty he condemns. An encounter with an old man becomes an exercise in humiliation rather than compassion. Shrike keeps turning religion, art, nature, and escape into cynical speeches, while his own marriage exposes the emptiness behind his performances. Miss Lonelyhearts joins Shrike and Mary in an outing whose promise of relief gives way to aggression and disorder. His search for a pure response to pain remains blocked by his urge to dominate the very people with whom he tries to connect.

Miss Lonelyhearts briefly goes to the country with Betty, where ordinary work and affection suggest a simpler life, but he returns to the city and the column. He meets Peter Doyle, a disabled reader who communicates his loneliness with painful directness. Miss Lonelyhearts feels a genuine identification with him and visits the Doyle home. There he meets Fay Doyle, whose advances pull him into a confused and violent sexual encounter. Instead of becoming the healing contact he imagined, the visit repeats the pattern by which pity, desire, and disgust turn into harm.

After further social humiliation and emotional collapse, Miss Lonelyhearts retreats from the newspaper world and falls ill. Emerging from his fever, he believes that his previously fragmented religious longing has become certainty and that he can answer suffering through unconditional love. Peter Doyle approaches with a gun after Fay has portrayed Miss Lonelyhearts as her attacker. Miss Lonelyhearts sees Doyle as the first person upon whom he can act out his new vision and runs to embrace him. Doyle resists, the gun discharges, and the two men fall down the stairs together. The hoped-for miracle ends as another act of violence, and the novella closes without separating spiritual aspiration from madness and destruction.

characters.description: A former teacher whose popular book about psychology has made her a reluctant public authority on human behavior. Visiting a women's physical-training college to give a lecture, she enjoys the students' company and the flattering belief that her insight can explain people.
characters.name: Lucy Pym

characters.description: The formidable principal of Leys, the residential college where young women train to teach physical education. An old friend of Lucy's, she is proud of the school's discipline, standards, and close community and persuades Lucy to extend her visit.
characters.name: Henrietta Hodge

characters.description: A senior member of the Leys staff whose brisk competence and demanding standards reflect the school's emphasis on physical precision. She helps supervise the students through the pressure of their final term.
characters.name: Miss Lux

characters.description: A member of the Leys staff involved in the daily administration and observation of college life. Her familiarity with its routines helps Lucy understand the enclosed world she has entered.
characters.name: Miss Wragg

characters.description: An outstanding senior student at Leys, admired for her steadiness, generosity, and natural authority. She appears well suited to the work for which the college is preparing her and is widely liked by students and staff.
characters.name: Mary Innes

characters.description: A determined senior student whose future depends heavily on professional success. Conscientious and ambitious, she feels the strain of assessment and of competing for the limited appointments available after graduation.
characters.name: Rouse

characters.description: A Brazilian student at Leys whose emotional directness and outsider's perspective distinguish her from many of her English classmates. She is intensely loyal to the people she loves and makes little effort to hide strong feeling.
characters.name: Desterro

characters.description: A self-possessed and socially prominent Leys student known by the nickname Beau. Her confidence and place within the student hierarchy help Lucy read the friendships, loyalties, and tensions of the senior group.
characters.name: Beau Nash

recaps.ending: Lucy concludes that the gymnasium accident was not accidental: Rouse, resentful over the decision that favored Mary Innes for a coveted appointment, tampered with equipment and caused Mary's devastating fall. Lucy had information that could have exposed Rouse but withheld it, persuading herself that a young life should not be ruined by one act. Before that private choice can settle matters, Rouse is found dead. The death appears self-inflicted, but Lucy recognizes that Desterro, fiercely devoted to Mary, killed Rouse in revenge and arranged the scene. Lucy now sees that her effort to dispose mercifully of the first wrongdoing enabled a second and fatal one. Rather than expose Desterro, she remains silent again and leaves Leys. The college's polished order survives publicly, but Mary has been gravely injured, Rouse is dead, and Lucy departs stripped of confidence in both her psychological authority and her right to decide justice for others.
recaps.in_short: Successful popular psychologist Lucy Pym visits Leys, a rigorous women's physical-training college run by her old friend Henrietta Hodge. Charmed by the students, Lucy stays through the tense final weeks of examinations, demonstrations, and job appointments. Competition for a desirable post creates resentment when the admired Mary Innes is favored over the ambitious Rouse. Mary then suffers a catastrophic fall during gymnasium work. Lucy realizes that Rouse tampered with equipment, but suppresses what she knows, hoping to spare Rouse and preserve the community. Rouse is subsequently found dead in what looks like suicide. Lucy understands that Desterro, whose loyalty to Mary is absolute, killed Rouse in revenge. Her first act of private mercy has helped make another death possible. Lucy leaves without revealing Desterro, no longer trusting the easy authority her reputation as a psychologist gave her.

recaps.text: Lucy Pym, unexpectedly famous after writing a successful book on psychology, travels to Leys to lecture. The residential college trains young women for careers in physical education and is run by Lucy's old friend Henrietta Hodge. Lucy expects a brief professional visit but is flattered by the welcome and intrigued by the disciplined, energetic student community. She agrees to stay longer. The apparent health and order of Leys contrast with the private pressures of its final term, when senior students face examinations, public demonstrations, and decisions that will determine their first jobs.

As Lucy observes lessons and shares the college routine, individual students emerge from the group. Mary Innes is admired for balance, ability, and kindness; Rouse is serious, ambitious, and acutely conscious that achievement will shape her future; Desterro is emotionally direct and intensely loyal; Beau Nash occupies a confident social position. Lucy enjoys applying her psychological ideas to them, but much of what she learns comes through ordinary companionship rather than theory. Beneath the camaraderie, fatigue and competition grow as staff assess the seniors and outside appointments become the measure of years of work.

The award of a particularly desirable professional post sharpens existing tensions. Henrietta and the staff choose Mary Innes, valuing her character and suitability as well as technical performance. Rouse has strong reasons to believe that diligence and results should have secured the opportunity for her, and the decision leaves her bitter. Lucy sees that the college's ideal of fair, impersonal judgment cannot remove the personal consequences of choosing one student over another. Preparations continue for the final displays, with demanding apparatus work taking place under pressure while loyalty to Mary and resentment over the appointment divide feelings within the senior group.

During gymnasium work, Mary suffers a terrible fall and is left gravely injured, destroying the professional future that had just opened to her. The incident is treated as an accident, but details noticed by Lucy indicate that equipment was deliberately tampered with. Her observations lead her to Rouse, whose resentment over Mary's appointment supplied a motive. Lucy now holds information that could turn a college tragedy into a criminal accusation. Tempted to regard the sabotage as a single desperate act rather than the whole measure of Rouse's character, she withholds what she knows and allows the official account of accident to stand.

Rouse is found dead, and the circumstances suggest suicide driven by guilt. Lucy, however, understands that Desterro killed her in revenge for Mary's injury and arranged the death to conceal the act. Lucy's earlier silence protected Rouse from exposure but also left punishment to someone whose fierce loyalty admitted no restraint. Faced with the consequences of her attempt at private mercy, Lucy again chooses not to disclose what she knows. Leys can preserve an outward account in which one accident is followed by one suicide, but Mary remains gravely harmed and Rouse is dead. Lucy leaves the college chastened, recognizing that her reputation for understanding motives did not grant her the wisdom or authority to dispose of other people's guilt.

recaps.ending: Operation Oyster Bay has destroyed Manticore's main orbital industry, much of Grayson's Blackbird complex, and millions of lives, including most of Honor's extended family and Andrew LaFollet. Manticore retains enough ships and missiles to defeat Filareta's approaching Solarian fleet, but doing so alone would consume scarce ammunition before industry can recover. Pritchart reaches Manticoran space with Theisman, Zilwicki, Cachat, and Simoes. She confirms that Haven officials altered the correspondence that restarted the war and presents evidence that the Mesa Alignment engineered the wider conflict and Oyster Bay. Honor finds Simoes sincere within the limits of his knowledge. Elizabeth and Pritchart end the Manticore-Haven war and form a military alliance. Haven's nearby fleet will help meet Filareta, while both governments face reconstruction, lingering distrust, and an enemy whose hidden base, fleet, technology, and Renaissance Factor network remain largely unknown.
recaps.in_short: As the Solarian League moves toward war over New Tuscany, Honor Harrington carries a peace offer to Haven and President Pritchart opens negotiations. At Spindle, Michelle Henke uses Apollo missiles to defeat a vastly larger Solarian force, but the secret Mesa Alignment then executes Operation Oyster Bay. Its undetectable weapons destroy Manticore's orbital industry, devastate Grayson's Blackbird yards, and kill millions, including Andrew LaFollet and most of Honor's extended family. The League exploits Manticore's losses by sending more than four hundred wallers under Filareta. Meanwhile, Zilwicki and Cachat return with Mesa defector Simoes and evidence of the Alignment's long campaign of manipulation. Pritchart secretly brings that evidence to Manticore and admits that Haven officials falsified the correspondence that restarted the war. Elizabeth ends the war with Haven and accepts Pritchart's offer of a joint fleet against Filareta and the still-hidden Alignment.

recaps.text: Previously: Manticore and Haven remain at war after falsified diplomatic correspondence destroyed their last attempt at peace. Each government believes the other manipulated the exchanges, and the resulting campaign culminated in the Battle of Manticore. Honor Harrington's victory left Manticore with a decisive missile advantage and Haven's senior commander Lester Tourville as a prisoner, but it did not resolve the dispute over responsibility. Elsewhere, attacks linked to Manpower and Mesa have drawn Manticore into a widening struggle across the Talbott region. At New Tuscany, Solarian Admiral Bing destroyed three Manticoran destroyers without provocation. Michelle Henke, serving as Vice Admiral Goldpeak, destroyed Bing's flagship and forced the surviving Solarian force to surrender its intact records. Manticore now possesses evidence supporting its account, but the incident threatens direct conflict with the far larger Solarian League just as Queen Elizabeth seeks a way to end the war with Haven.

The Solarian League receives Manticore's report on New Tuscany and captured records supporting the charge that Admiral Bing opened fire first. Civilian leaders favor a measured reply, but Fleet Admiral Rajampet begins preparing for war and urges an eventual attack on Manticore. Queen Elizabeth and Honor conclude that the growing League crisis makes peace with Haven strategically urgent. Honor prepares to travel as Elizabeth's representative and consults the captured Lester Tourville about Haven's leadership. On Grayson, Protector Benjamin Mayhew and High Admiral Matthews defend the Manticoran alliance against domestic critics while acknowledging the League's immense long-term strength. Unknown to Manticore, Alignment Commodore Carol Ostby has penetrated the binary system with stealth ships. His force maps orbital targets for Operation Oyster Bay and plans a final targeting relay for a mass missile strike.

Solarian analysts possess evidence that Manticoran missiles far outrange accepted limits, but their superiors resist the conclusion. On Mesa, Albrecht Detweiler learns that Zilwicki and his Haven partner vanished during a security disaster. The Alignment decides to blame them and the anti-slavery movement for the Green Pines explosions while using forged material to obscure Mesa's role at New Tuscany. Detweiler expects Oyster Bay to begin within months. At Manticore's Weyland research station, new attention to evacuation readiness exposes serious weaknesses. Honor then arrives outside Haven with Eighth Fleet and receives safe conduct from President Pritchart. As Queen Elizabeth's plenipotentiary, she offers negotiations backed by a warning that Manticore can systematically destroy Haven's navy and orbital industry if talks fail. Pritchart's cabinet accepts that negotiation is necessary to preserve the republic, though admitting the truth about the falsified correspondence could carry a heavy domestic cost.

An Alignment scout force at Grayson narrowly avoids detection while conducting Oyster Bay reconnaissance. Honor opens formal peace talks with an expanded Haven delegation, arguing that permanent security cannot rest on Manticore's present technological superiority. At Spindle, Michelle Henke prepares Tenth Fleet for a possible Solarian assault and tests Apollo tactics. Junior officers also recognize that released evidence and independent reporting may help prevent the League from building political support for war. Meanwhile, Alignment forces begin placing hidden missile pods near Manticore. Operative Baltazar Juppe gives journalist Audrey O'Hanrahan forged New Tuscany records designed to survive scrutiny and make Manticore appear to have fired first. O'Hanrahan agrees to investigate the material rather than publish immediately. Queen Elizabeth confronts Catherine Montaigne over Green Pines. Montaigne denies that Anton Zilwicki would attack civilians but reveals that he secretly traveled to Mesa, making the false accusation against him more difficult to rebut.

Montaigne explains that Zilwicki and a Haven operative went to Mesa to investigate Manpower and then disappeared. Honor privately gives Pritchart the same context, and Haven's own records corroborate that its missing officer had blamed an outside power for earlier attacks. Both governments treat Green Pines as disinformation intended to derail peace. At Spindle, reconnaissance finds a Solarian force of seventy-one superdreadnoughts and many escorts approaching under an admiral committed to punitive action. Henke conceals her strength, prepares Apollo ammunition, and plans to fight if the force violates Manticoran territory. The Solarian commander dismisses warnings about Manticoran range, crosses the territorial limit, and demands Henke, her ships, and reparations. Governor Medusa refuses to yield. The ultimatum leaves Spindle facing invasion, while apparently authentic forged reports spread the claim that Manticore caused New Tuscany.

The Solarian ultimatum expires and the invading force advances toward Flax. Henke's distributed scouts provide near-real-time targeting while hidden cruisers, ammunition ships, LAC carriers, and newly arrived units bracket the slower superdreadnoughts. Although Solarian staff officers detect anomalies and warn of concealed missile pods, their commander remains certain that numerical superiority will prevail. At Point Longbow, twelve Manticoran cruisers launch more than twelve thousand weapons. Apollo control links reshape the attack against Solarian defenses, which stop only a small fraction of the missiles. The opening salvo destroys or cripples twenty-three superdreadnoughts, including the flagship. Before the prepared follow-up attack is needed, the surviving force drops its wedges and surrenders. Manticore has won the battle in a single exchange, but must now secure damaged ships, rescue survivors, and control an enormous prisoner population.

Goldpeak grants the surrendered Solarians prisoner-of-war treatment and organizes their removal from ships that Manticore lacks crews to operate. Abigail Hearns leads a dangerous search-and-rescue party into a wrecked superdreadnought while Marines secure other prizes without renewed fighting. In Haven, an obstructionist legislator stalls the peace talks for domestic advantage, but Honor continues to distinguish political maneuvering from Pritchart and Theisman's genuine desire for peace. News of Spindle reaches the negotiators and deepens the strategic crisis. Manticore's leaders conclude that the League may ignore the evidence and use the defeat to justify escalation. Queen Elizabeth therefore treats the states as effectively at war, closes Manticoran-controlled wormholes to Solarian traffic, recalls merchant shipping, and prepares broader economic measures. Direct action against Mesa remains under consideration, but has not been ordered.

Manticore begins implementing its junction closures as Home Fleet rebuilds under the weight of earlier losses. Andrew LaFollet prepares unusually detailed security for an outing involving Honor's infant son Raoul and close relatives. At Weyland, an evacuation exercise becomes a real station evacuation, disrupting work but exposing and correcting dangerous readiness failures. At the same time, the concealed Oyster Bay force completes its deployment. Its spider-drive ships have placed missile pods throughout the Manticore binary and at Grayson without detection because their propulsion produces none of the familiar long-range signature. Six synchronized attacks begin. Grazer torpedoes and other weapons approach vital infrastructure while Manticoran defenders receive only an unexplained encrypted transmission. Honor's family sets out under armored escort, unaware that the coordinated strike is already in progress.

Operation Oyster Bay strikes without effective warning. Grazers tear apart Hephaestus and Vulcan, destroying docked warships, manufacturing sections, and millions of people within seconds. Follow-on missiles eliminate most dispersed orbital yards and much of Manticore's skilled industrial workforce. The attackers avoid deliberate planetary bombardment, but the wreckage creates its own catastrophe. A ready-duty tug destroys or captures several fragments headed for Sphinx, yet others reach the surface. Ocean impacts devastate coastal areas, and a massive fragment obliterates Yawata Crossing. During the emergency, Andrew LaFollet orders the air car carrying Allison Harrington and Raoul down, secures the infant in an armored carrier, and ejects Allison in a survival shell as destruction approaches. Manticore's orbital industry is shattered, and the full human cost on the planets is still emerging.

Elizabeth's emergency council learns that Hephaestus, Vulcan, and Weyland are gone, along with almost all heavy construction and missile production. Weyland's earlier evacuation saves much of its workforce and off-site records preserve research, but Manticore cannot quickly replace the lost plant or millions of skilled workers. Civilian deaths on Sphinx rise into the millions, and treecat clans also suffer. Caparelli and Givens accept institutional responsibility, though the government recognizes that the unknown attacker used a purpose-built technology no existing defense anticipated. White Haven argues that the Solarian League had little reason to undermine its own numerical advantage this way and identifies Manpower as the leading, unproved suspect. Manticore expects future arrivals to leave detectable hyper footprints and plans denser surveillance. Elizabeth refuses surrender. In the League, senior officials answer Spindle with propaganda and rearmament while privately planning a later war, then receive an urgent report concerning Manticore whose contents are not yet disclosed.

Solarian analysts Al-Fanudahi and Teague warn that Oyster Bay reveals an unknown power whose ambitions may extend beyond Manticore, but senior planners see an opportunity to attack while Manticore is weakened. Haven learns of the disaster and suspends peace talks when Honor and Eighth Fleet are recalled. Pritchart's cabinet refuses to assume the attacker is Haven's ally and increasingly suspects coordinated outside manipulation involving Mesa or Manpower. Honor returns to the ruined home system and learns the personal cost: the Yawata Crossing strike killed most of her extended family. Her mother and Raoul survived because Andrew LaFollet evacuated them, but LaFollet and Jeremiah died when their vehicle was hit. Judah Yanukov then reports that Oyster Bay also destroyed Grayson's Blackbird shipyards, killed nearly the entire workforce there, and killed High Admiral Matthews. Yanukov succeeds him, while both allied industrial bases face reconstruction.

Rajampet authorizes an offensive beginning with almost four hundred Solarian wallers under Fleet Admiral Filareta, followed by an even larger second wave if necessary. Manticore's ammunition shortage forces Michelle Henke to return her Apollo pods and conserve what remains. A trusted Beowulf channel warns both Manticore and Haven of the coming attack. Manticore can defeat Filareta tactically, but Honor warns that the missile expenditure would leave the realm unable to sustain operations while the League adapts and outproduces it. In Haven, Linda Traney argues that Beowulf's warning may be intended to preserve the peace process, though anti-negotiation factions could instead exploit Manticore's weakness. Filareta begins assembling more than four hundred wallers. He does not fully share his staff's confidence that Oyster Bay has made Manticore helpless, but proceeds under orders.

At the hidden Darius base, Albrecht Detweiler welcomes the returning Oyster Bay force and confirms the Alignment's responsibility. Its prototype shark-class ships and larger vessels under construction form a covert navy commanded by his son Benjamin. Because Manticore is now alert and the trained crews are irreplaceable, Benjamin persuades Albrecht not to risk another immediate strike. The Alignment instead activates its long-prepared political plan. Families planted across allied systems will present themselves as established anti-slavery leaders, encourage frontier secessions as the Solarian League fractures, and assemble the Renaissance Factor as an apparently defensive successor bloc. The connection to Mesa and the Alignment's genetic program will remain hidden while the organization exploits the League's broader military and political collapse.

Anton Zilwicki and Victor Cachat return alive with Mesa scientist Herlander Simoes. Their account gives Pritchart's government credible grounds to investigate a centuries-old Alignment, its spider drive, and its manipulation of interstellar conflicts. Pritchart concludes that the same conspiracy may explain both Haven's falsified diplomatic traffic and Oyster Bay. As Filareta approaches, Elizabeth publicly rejects surrender and promises that Manticore will resist. Pritchart then enters Manticoran space secretly with Theisman, Zilwicki, Cachat, and Simoes. She admits that Yves Rochlaude and Arnold Giancola altered Haven's side of the correspondence that restarted the war and presents evidence tying the Alignment to the broader campaign. Honor judges Simoes sincere within the limits of his knowledge. Elizabeth and Pritchart declare the Manticore-Haven war over. Haven offers its nearby fleet against Filareta, allowing Manticore to conserve missiles, and the former enemies form an alliance against the immediate Solarian attack and the still-hidden Alignment.
